title: Arrays & Strings
summary: A row of equal-sized slots packed in memory — the one structure that maps straight onto how hardware addresses RAM, and the base layer under half the interview world.

blocks.markdown:
An array is a row of equal-sized slots packed back-to-back in memory.

- Slot `i` sits at `base + i × size`, so reading any index is **O(1)** — no scanning.
- **Insert or delete in the middle is O(n)**: every later element shifts. The end is cheap.
- A **dynamic array** (list, vector, slice) grows by copying into a bigger block, giving **O(1) amortized** append.
- A **string** is just an array of characters — often immutable.

blocks.subTitle: When to reach for it
blocks.markdown:
Default to an array; pick a variant when the access pattern demands it.

| Situation | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Lookup by position, bounded size | Plain array |
| Grows, mostly append at end | Dynamic array |
| Many range-sum queries | Prefix-sum array |
| Many range updates | Difference array |

blocks.subTitle: Contiguous memory
blocks.markdown:
Arrays exist because RAM is one giant numbered sequence of bytes, and hardware is great at "give me address X."

- Put `n` equal-sized items in a row from a base address; item `i` lives at `base + i × size`.
- The CPU computes that address with one multiply-and-add — that *is* O(1) access.
- **Cache locality** is the quiet bonus: the CPU pulls a whole 64-byte line, so neighbors are already loaded.
- This is why an array scan often beats a "clever" pointer structure ([a06-linked-lists](a06-linked-lists.md)).

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic arrays & doubling
blocks.markdown:
A dynamic array tracks **size** (used) and **capacity** (allocated). Append is free until full, then it doubles and copies.

![Array contiguous memory and dynamic-array doubling](assets/a02-arrays-strings/array-memory-and-doubling.svg)

- On overflow: allocate **2× capacity**, copy all elements (O(n)), then write.
- Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, n, summing to ≈ **2n** total work over n appends.
- That averages to **O(1) amortized** per append — doubling is what keeps the series finite.

assets.alt: Array contiguous memory and dynamic-array doubling

blocks.subTitle: The cost table
blocks.markdown:
The end of an array is cheap; the middle is expensive.

| Operation | Time |
|---|---|
| Access / update `arr[i]` | O(1) |
| Append at end | O(1) amortized |
| Insert/delete middle | O(n) |
| Search unsorted | O(n) |

Inserting at `k` slides every later element right — `n − k` moves. Sorted search drops to O(log n) via binary search ([a16-binary-search](a16-binary-search.md)).

blocks.subTitle: Strings & immutability
blocks.markdown:
A string is a char array, so `s[i]` is O(1) — but in Java, Python, JS, C# strings are **immutable**.

```python
# BAD: O(n^2) — each += copies the whole growing string
result = ""
for word in words:
    result = result + word

# GOOD: O(n) — buffer, then one join
buffer = []
for word in words:
    buffer.append(word)
result = "".join(buffer)
```

- Every "edit" builds a new string and copies it — O(n) each.
- Concatenating in a loop is quietly **O(n²)**; use a builder/buffer.

blocks.subTitle: Prefix sums & difference arrays
blocks.markdown:
Precompute running totals once and every range-sum query becomes one subtraction.

![Prefix-sum array and a range-sum query](assets/a02-arrays-strings/prefix-sum-range-query.svg)

- Build `P` where `P[k]` = sum of the first k elements (`P[0] = 0`, length n+1).
- `rangeSum(l, r) = P[r+1] − P[l]` — **O(1)** per query after an O(n) build.
- The mirror trick: a **difference array** makes many *range updates* cheap (`D[l] += x`, `D[r+1] -= x`, then prefix-sum).

assets.alt: Prefix-sum array and a range-sum query

blocks.subTitle: In-place patterns
blocks.markdown:
"In-place" means **O(1) extra memory** — rearrange with a few variables, not a second array.

- **Two pointers from the ends** — swap toward the middle to reverse or check a palindrome.
- **Read/write pointers** — a `write` index trails a scanning `read`, copying only keepers (remove zeros/dupes).
- **Reversal trick for rotation** — reverse all, reverse first `k`, reverse the rest. O(n) time, O(1) space.

More in [a04-two-pointers-sliding-window](a04-two-pointers-sliding-window.md).

blocks.subTitle: Array vs linked list
blocks.markdown:
They share the "sequence" idea but have opposite cost profiles.

| Aspect | Array | Linked list |
|---|---|---|
| Index | O(1) | O(n) |
| Middle insert | O(n) | O(1) given node |
| Cache | Friendly | Pointer-chasing |

Arrays win most real workloads thanks to locality. Reach for a list only when you insert/delete a lot at a held position.

blocks.subTitle: Precompute or not
blocks.markdown:
Prefix sums and difference arrays trade O(n) memory and a one-time build for O(1) per op afterward.

- Worth it only with **many** queries/updates — for a single query, just loop.
- If the array **changes between queries**, you need a Fenwick or segment tree ([a20-intervals-sweep-line](a20-intervals-sweep-line.md)).
- Sorting first costs O(n log n) but unlocks binary search and two-pointer patterns — pay it when you search repeatedly.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
The dynamic arrays you use daily tune the doubling trade-off differently.

- **CPython `list`** — array of pointers, grows ~1.125× plus a constant; `list.insert(0, x)` is O(n), so use `deque` for the front.
- **Java `ArrayList`** grows ~1.5×; **`StringBuilder`** exists because `String` is immutable — turns loop concat from O(n²) to O(n).
- **Go slices** are `{ptr, len, cap}`; `append` may reallocate, so always `s = append(s, x)`.
- **Columnar engines** (Arrow, ClickHouse) store columns contiguously for cache-friendly scans.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Indexing is O(1), so arrays are all fast."** Only *access* is; middle insert and unsorted search are O(n).
- **"Resizing makes append slow."** Per-resize is O(n), but append is **O(1) amortized** — don't confuse worst case with average.
- **`s += c` in a loop.** Quietly O(n²) in immutable-string languages; use a builder.
- **Prefix-sum off-by-one.** `P` has length n+1; `rangeSum = P[r+1] − P[l]`, not `P[r] − P[l]`.
- **Mutating an array while iterating by index** shifts elements and skips items — iterate backward.
